summary: Defines a convention for carrying SNMP packets over the transport provided by Novell's IPX protocol. This lets management stations talk to agents on IPX networks. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1420.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1298 describes how SNMP messages can travel over IPX instead of UDP. It assigns IPX socket numbers to message types and explains how an IPX address can be represented.

questions: how does snmp run over ipx
subtitle: A convention for carrying SNMP messages through the IPX transport.

tldr.problem: Some environments did not have UDP transport available, but still needed to carry SNMP management messages over IPX.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns IPX sockets to SNMP requests and traps, and specifies an IPX address representation for management information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1298 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1420.

today: RFC 1298 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1420.

sections.title: Why Carry SNMP over IPX
sections.content:
SNMP is a protocol for managing network devices. The RFC describes carrying SNMP over the connectionless, unacknowledged datagram service provided by IPX. It notes that UDP was the common transport for SNMP in the Internet and cautions that choosing another transport can affect interoperability.

The document is a convention for environments where UDP transport services are unavailable. It does not change the SNMP messages themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP messages can be carried by IPX when UDP is unavailable. The SNMP message stays the same, but using a different transport can limit compatibility with other systems.

sections.title: IPX Sockets for SNMP Messages
sections.content:
IPX packets carrying SNMP set the IPX Packet Type field to 4. SNMP GetRequest, GetNextRequest, and SetRequest messages use destination socket 36879, also written as hexadecimal 900F. Trap messages use destination socket 36880, or hexadecimal 9010.

A GetResponse returns to the IPX address and socket that sent its corresponding request.
sections.plainLanguage: Requests use IPX socket 36879, while traps use socket 36880. A response goes back to the address and socket that sent the request.

sections.title: Packet Size and IPX Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that implementations support SNMP messages up to 546 bytes, the maximum IPX packet size. That size is guaranteed to pass through IPX routers that do not fragment packets. Longer packets may be used when the path's maximum is known. For a trap sent by an IPX agent, the agent-addr field should contain 0.0.0.0; a manager can ask the transport layer for the source.

The RFC also defines an IPX transport address as 12 octets: a 4-octet network number, a 6-octet physical address, and a 2-octet socket number, in network-byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: IPX supports packets up to 546 bytes without fragmentation across routers that do not fragment. An IPX address in this format has a network number, a physical address, and a socket number.
